content: Chocolate is a solid edible product made by combining cocoa solids, cocoa butter (or oil), and finely powdered sugar. The specific proportions of these ingredients vary depending on the recipe, resulting in different types of chocolate. In some cases, the use of specific names for chocolate products is regulated by governmental standards. Terminology The products derived from cacao beans, which are used to make chocolate, are referred to by different names in various parts of the world. In the American chocolate industry: Chocolate liquor refers to the ground or melted state of the cacao bean nib. Cocoa butter is the fat component of the cacao bean. Cocoa powder is the non-fat portion of the cacao bean, ground into a fine powder. Classification Chocolate is a widely used ingredient and comes in many forms and flavors. Variations in the quantities of ingredients, as well as the time and temperature of roasting the beans, result in different flavors and types of chocolate. Unsweetened chocolate is pure chocolate liquor, also known as bitter or baking chocolate. It is mixed with some form of fat to create a solid substance. This type of chocolate is unadulterated, made from pure, ground, roasted cacao beans, and has a strong, deep chocolate flavor. When sugar is added, it serves as a base for cakes, brownies, confections, and cookies. Dark chocolate is made by adding fat and sugar to cacao. It does not contain milk as an additive and is sometimes referred to as plain chocolate. In the U.S., it is called sweet chocolate and must contain at least 15% chocolate liquor. European regulations require a minimum of 35% cocoa solids. Milk chocolate contains milk powder or condensed milk in addition to chocolate. U.S. regulations require a minimum of 10% chocolate liquor, while EU standards specify at least 25% cocoa solids. Milk chocolate was first solidified in the 1870s by Swiss confectioner Daniel Peter, using condensed milk invented by Henri Nestlé. The Hershey process, developed by Milton S. Hershey, allows milk chocolate to be produced more economically by making it less sensitive to the freshness of milk. Experts believe the milk is partially lipolyzed, producing butyric acid, which stabilizes the milk and gives the chocolate a tangy taste. This flavor, familiar to the American public, is now replicated by other manufacturers by adding butyric acid to their milk chocolates. Semisweet chocolate is a type of dark chocolate with a lower sugar content, typically used for cooking. It usually contains about half the sugar of regular chocolate. Bittersweet chocolate is made from chocolate liquor (or unsweetened chocolate) with added sugar (typically one-third), more cocoa butter, vanilla, and sometimes lecithin. It contains less sugar and more liquor than semisweet chocolate, but the two are interchangeable in baking. Both bittersweet and semisweet chocolates are sometimes referred to as couverture, which contains at least 32% cocoa butter. Many brands now label their products with the percentage of cocoa content, which includes chocolate liquor and added cocoa butter. Generally, the higher the cocoa percentage, the less sweet the chocolate. Couverture chocolate is a term for chocolates rich in cocoa butter. Popular brands of couverture used by professional pastry chefs include Valrhona, Felchlin, Lindt & Sprüngli, Scharffen Berger, Cacao Barry, Callebaut, and Guittard. These chocolates often contain 70% or more cocoa and have a total fat content of 30-40%. White chocolate is a confection made from sugar and fat (either cocoa butter or vegetable oils) without cocoa solids. Cocoa powder comes in two types: natural cocoa and Dutch-processed cocoa. Both are made by pulverizing partially defatted chocolate liquor and removing nearly all the cocoa butter. Natural cocoa is light in color, somewhat acidic, and has a strong chocolate flavor. It is commonly used in recipes that call for baking soda, as the alkalinity of baking soda reacts with the acidity of natural cocoa to create leavening. Dutch-processed cocoa is treated with alkali to neutralize its natural acidity, resulting in a milder taste and a deeper, warmer color. It is often used for chocolate drinks like hot chocolate due to its ease of blending with liquids. However, Dutch processing destroys most of the flavonols present in cocoa. Compound chocolate is a technical term for a confection that combines cocoa with vegetable fat, often tropical fats or hydrogenated fats, as a replacement for cocoa butter. It is primarily used for candy bar coatings. In the U.S., it cannot legally be called chocolate because it lacks cocoa butter. Instead, it is often labeled with terms like chocolatey. Many candy bars in the U.S. no longer contain true chocolate as a major component, especially white chocolate, which may not contain any cacao-derived ingredients. This substitution can result in inferior taste, texture, and potential health concerns, particularly when partially hydrogenated oils are used instead of cocoa butter. Flavor Additions and Variations Flavors such as mint, vanilla, coffee, orange, or strawberry are sometimes added to chocolate in creamy forms or as small pieces. Chocolate bars often include additional ingredients like peanuts, nuts, fruit, caramel, or crisped rice. Chocolate pieces in various flavors are also mixed with cereals to enhance their taste. Regulatory Definitions The FDA regulates the naming and ingredients of cacao products. Chocolate is defined as a product based on cocoa solids and/or cocoa fat. The specific amounts and types of cocoa solids and fat required for a product to be called chocolate are often debated. Manufacturers may use the term for cheaper variations containing less cocoa and more substitutes, which may not taste as good. In the EU, disagreements over the definition of chocolate have included issues such as the types of fat used and the quantity of cocoa. In 1999, the EU resolved the fat issue by allowing up to 5% of a chocolate product's content to consist of alternative fats like illipe, palm oil, sal, shea, kokum gurgi, or mango kernel. A recent workaround by the U.S. confection industry involves reducing the amount of cocoa butter in candy bars without using vegetable fats by adding polyglycerol polyricinoleate (PGPR), an artificial castor oil-derived emulsifier that mimics the mouthfeel of fat. Up to 3% PGPR may be added to chocolate for this purpose.
